measures.existing_conditions: The building’s HVAC systems operate using a mixture of local controls and a legacy building automation system (BAS) that provides limited monitoring capability. The control platform has not been comprehensively updated or recalibrated for several years, and the level of integration varies across equipment. Many components operate with minimal feedback, limited scheduling capability, and reduced visibility into equipment performance. Legacy or partially obsolete control devices are difficult to maintain, prone to failures, and may no longer be fully supported by the manufacturer.
measures.notes: Modernise the existing BAS and field devices onto an open digital platform with full feedback, trending and alarms to improve reliability, visibility and HVAC optimisation opportunities.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends implementing a comprehensive BAS upgrade to provide modern, centralized control and monitoring of all major HVAC systems. The retrofit would consolidate the existing control infrastructure into a unified digital platform capable of advanced sequencing, optimized scheduling, remote monitoring, trending, and alarms. Outdated control devices would be replaced with new DDC components. A non-proprietary framework such as Niagara 4 is recommended to allow future expansion and easier maintenance. The upgraded BAS is expected to reduce energy use, improve comfort, and extend equipment service life. Enbridge Gas incentive programs for advanced building controls can help offset capital costs and improve project payback.

measures.existing_conditions: The existing piping arrangement separates the WSHP loop, primary heating loop, and domestic hot water (DHW) loop into independent hydronic systems, each served by dedicated boilers and pumping configurations. The primary heating loop operates at higher temperatures for space heating, the WSHP loop operates at lower temperatures, and the DHW system functions on a separate loop without hydraulic or control integration. This configuration increases system complexity and limits opportunities for load diversity, heat recovery, and coordinated temperature optimization. During shoulder seasons, independent loop operation can contribute to boiler short cycling, elevated supply temperatures, and reduced overall plant efficiency.
measures.measure_title: Primary–Secondary Boiler and Hydronic Loop Reconfiguration (Primary loop + WSHP loop + DHW loop)
measures.notes: Reconfigure Primary heating loop, WSHP loop and DHW loop to a primary–secondary layout, hydraulically separating loops to improve temperature control, boiler protection and plant efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to evaluate reconfiguring the WSHP loop, primary heating loop, and DHW piping into a coordinated Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. Under a P-S configuration, a central boiler primary loop would maintain controlled supply temperatures while secondary loops draw only the required flow and temperature for each load. This arrangement provides hydraulic separation, allows differentiated temperature control for high- and low-temperature systems, improves outdoor-air reset effectiveness, and reduces short cycling. Improved integration may also enhance return-water temperature control, supporting more efficient boiler operation. When implemented in conjunction with condensing boiler upgrades, this redesign may allow optimization of boiler staging and potential reduction in total boiler count, thereby lowering long-term maintenance complexity and operating costs. Further engineering review is required to confirm detailed hydraulic configuration, load diversity assumptions, and control sequencing strategy.

measures.measure_title: MUA Retrofit Two (2) Option: Hydronic MUA with VFD / WSHP MUA with VFD
measures.notes: Upgrade the existing MUA system by adding VFD control and converting to either a hydronic or water-source heat pump configuration to improve energy efficiency. Qualify for Enbridge incentives.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Option 1 – Install VFDs and Convert existing MUA to Hydronic MUA
Mann recommends installing a new hydronic heating coil in the existing make-up air (MUA) unit, to be served by the central boiler plant. A modulating control valve would regulate heating-water flow to maintain corridor supply-air temperature.
As the existing MUA unit is currently operating without VFD control, new variable-frequency drives (VFDs) should be installed on the supply fan to enable proper airflow modulation. Once installed, the VFDs will be fully integrated into the BAS to provide optimized fan control, scheduling, and occupancy-based ventilation reduction.
Hydronic conversion also reduces maintenance requirements and qualifies for Enbridge incentives, improving overall project payback.

Option 2 – Install VFDs and Convert existing MUA to Water-Source Heat Pump (WSHP) MUA
Mann recommends converting the existing make-up air (MUA) unit to a water-source heat pump (WSHP) MUA unit. The new WSHP heating coil can be installed within the existing MUA cabinet, allowing the building to retain most of the original ventilation infrastructure. 
The existing WSHP loop piping can remain and be reused, and the boiler plant would continue to provide supplemental heat only when required. A WSHP-based heating coil is significantly more efficient than a gas-fired burner because it uses the thermal energy already present within the building—rather than generating heat through combustion. The WSHP coil is capable of providing heating whenever the ventilation system operates and can take advantage of heat already present in the hydronic loop, reducing boiler runtime and improving overall system efficiency. One consideration is that the MUA electrical load may increase slightly depending on the WSHP coil configuration; however, the improved efficiency and reduced gas usage often outweigh these impacts. 
During the heating season, the WSHP coil extracts heat from the hydronic loop and transfers it into the ventilation air stream. When more heat is required than is being generated within the building, the central boiler plant provides supplemental heat to maintain loop temperature. 
During warmer weather, suites operating in cooling mode can reject heat into the WSHP loop, supplying “free heat” to the MUA heating coil during mild outdoor conditions. During shoulder seasons, the system can recycle heat internally: heat removed from south-facing suites in cooling mode can offset ventilation heating demands from north-facing corridors, reducing the need for gas-fired heating entirely.

measures.existing_conditions:
The Cooling tower is equipped with constant-speed or multi-speed fan motors that operate at discrete speeds regardless of the actual cooling load. Under part-load conditions, the fans still consume close to full power, resulting in unnecessary electrical usage and increased wear on mechanical components.
In addition, the condenser water pumps operate at constant speed, with no VFDs installed. As a result, pump output does not modulate with system demand, leading to unnecessary electrical energy consumption and increased mechanical wear during part-load operation.
measures.measure_title: VFD Retrofit for cooling tower fan and Condenser water pumps
measures.notes: Install VFDs on the cooling tower fan motors, suite circulation pumps, and condenser water pumps to enable demand-based modulation, reduce electrical energy consumption during part-load operation, lower noise and mechanical wear, and improve overall system efficiency and reliability.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the cooling tower fan motors. VFDs will allow fan speed to be modulated based on condenser water temperature, ambient conditions or BAS commands, so airflow more closely matches the required cooling load. Reducing fan speed yields large electrical savings due to the cubic relationship between power and speed, while also reducing noise and extending equipment life.
In addition, it is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the condenser water pump. The VFDs would allow pump speed to be modulated based on system demand, pressure, or temperature requirements, enabling flow rates to more closely match actual operating conditions. Reducing pump speed during part-load operation would result in meaningful electrical energy savings, reduced mechanical wear, and improved system reliability. Controls, sensors, and associated safeties would need to be updated and properly commissioned as part of this measure.

measures.existing_conditions: Suite-level hydronic circulation pumps are currently operating at constant speed to deliver heating or cooling water to fan coil units. Flow is typically balanced using manual balancing valves or fixed control settings. As a result, the pumps operate at full speed regardless of actual thermal demand, leading to unnecessary energy consumption and increased mechanical wear during periods of partial load.
measures.notes: Convert constant-speed suite circulation pumps to VFD control to match flow with demand and reduce pump energy consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the suite-level circulation pumps to allow pump speed to modulate based on real-time demand. The VFD would adjust pump output in response to pressure differential or control valve position, enabling reduced flow during low-load conditions. This retrofit reduces electrical energy consumption, extends pump life, and improves hydronic system stability while maintaining adequate heating and cooling performance. Further engineering is required to confirm control strategy, sensor placement, and system compatibility.

measures.existing_conditions: The building is equipped with double-pane windows typical of its construction era. The windows were observed to be in generally fair condition at the time of the site visit. However, in aging buildings, the insulating glazing units (IGUs) may gradually lose performance over time due to seal deterioration and potential reduction of the insulating gas between panes. While no widespread failure was observed, long-term thermal performance may decline as glazing systems age.
measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of ongoing building envelope maintenance and long-term capital planning, it is recommended to monitor window performance and implement periodic re-caulking and weatherstripping renewal where required. Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

measures.existing_conditions: Common area lighting (e.g., corridors, stairwells, storage rooms, parking areas, and ancillary spaces) is primarily controlled through manual switches or time-based schedules, resulting in lighting operating during unoccupied periods. Limited occupancy-based control leads to unnecessary electrical energy use and increased lamp operating hours.
measures.notes: Install occupancy-based motion sensors for common area lighting to reduce unnecessary runtime, lower electrical consumption, and extend lighting equipment life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends installing occupancy / motion sensors to control common area lighting where appropriate. The motion sensors would automatically turn lighting on when spaces are occupied and off or dim when spaces are unoccupied, reducing unnecessary runtime while maintaining occupant safety and visibility.

This measure would reduce electrical energy consumption, extend lamp and ballast/driver life, and lower ongoing maintenance requirements. Motion control is particularly effective in intermittently occupied spaces such as stairwells, corridors, storage rooms, and parking areas.

Where applicable, motion sensors may be integrated with existing lighting control strategies or future centralized control systems to further enhance operational flexibility.

Under part-load conditions, the fans still consume close to full power, resulting in unnecessary electrical usage and increased wear on mechanical components.

measures.measure_title: VFD Retrofit for cooling tower fan and Condenser water pumps
measures.notes: Install VFDs on the cooling tower fan motors, suite circulation pumps, and condenser water pumps to enable demand-based modulation, reduce electrical energy consumption during part-load operation, lower noise and mechanical wear, and improve overall system efficiency and reliability.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the cooling tower fan motors. VFDs will allow fan speed to be modulated based on condenser water temperature, ambient conditions or BAS commands, so airflow more closely matches the required cooling load. Reducing fan speed yields large electrical savings due to the cubic relationship between power and speed, while also reducing noise and extending equipment life.
In addition, it is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the condenser water pump. The VFDs would allow pump speed to be modulated based on system demand, pressure, or temperature requirements, enabling flow rates to more closely match actual operating conditions. Reducing pump speed during part-load operation would result in meaningful electrical energy savings, reduced mechanical wear, and improved system reliability. Controls, sensors, and associated safeties would need to be updated and properly commissioned as part of this measure.

measures.retrofit_conditions:

Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

measures.notes: Install occupancy-based motion sensors for common area lighting to reduce unnecessary runtime, lower electrical consumption, and extend lighting equipment life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends installing occupancy / motion sensors to control common area lighting where appropriate. The motion sensors would automatically turn lighting on when spaces are occupied and off or dim when spaces are unoccupied, reducing unnecessary runtime while maintaining occupant safety and visibility.

This measure would reduce electrical energy consumption, extend lamp and ballast/driver life, and lower ongoing maintenance requirements. Motion control is particularly effective in intermittently occupied spaces such as stairwells, corridors, storage rooms, and parking areas.

Where applicable, motion sensors may be integrated with existing lighting control strategies or future centralized control systems to further enhance operational flexibility.

misc_items.text: The building envelope appears to be in generally good condition, with no significant signs of air leakage or deterioration observed at the time of the site visit. Envelope components appear to be performing as intended.

misc_items.text: The parking garage is served by a mechanical ventilation system controlled by carbon monoxide (CO) sensors. misc_items.text: The building includes an unheated parking garage, which is typical for buildings of this age. No dedicated space-heating system was observed, and garage temperatures are allowed to fluctuate with outdoor conditions.
misc_items.title: Unheated garage

misc_items.text: The building is served by a packaged domestic water booster pump system equipped with variable frequency drives (VFDs). The booster pump system was observed to be operating normally at the time of the site visit, with no abnormal noise, vibration, or visible mechanical deficiencies noted

A WSHP-based heating coil is significantly more efficient than a gas-fired burner because it uses the thermal energy already present within the building—rather than generating heat through combustion. During warmer weather, suites operating in cooling mode can reject heat into the WSHP loop, supplying “free heat” to the MUA heating coil during mild outdoor conditions. During shoulder seasons, the system can recycle heat internally: heat removed from south-facing suites in cooling mode can offset ventilation heating demands from north-facing corridors, reducing the need for gas-fired heating entirely.

ventilation_items.text:
The units are equipped with supply fans with variable frequency drives (VFDs), integral gas-fired heating burners, and DX cooling sections. The VFD, gas-fired heating burner, and DX Cooling coil were observed to be in fair to good condition.

Equipment appeared to be functioning as intended during the site walkthrough, with no visible signs of mechanical distress.

ventilation_items.text:
Although the MUA units are in generally good mechanical condition, the building is not equipped with a centralized Building Automation System (BAS) to coordinate MUA operation with the rest of the mechanical systems.

Integration of the existing VFD-controlled MUA units into a BAS would enable improved scheduling, supply air temperature reset, demand-based ventilation, and alarm monitoring. These enhancements would improve overall energy performance, operational oversight, and long-term system reliability.
